title: We Do This 'til We Free Us: Abolitionist Organizing and Transforming Justice
author: Mariame Kaba
target_audience: Activists and organizers interested in prison abolition
Students and scholars of social justice and political science
Readers seeking alternatives to policing and incarceration
Anyone interested in transformative and restorative justice
primary_purpose: To provide a radical vision and practical pathways for ending mass incarceration and policing, and to inspire and equip readers to build movements that center transformative justice and community care.

structure_format.organization: Collection of essays, interviews, and conversations organized thematically
features: Examples from the author’s organizing experience

key_concepts_lessons: Abolition is both a vision and a practice rooted in community care and transformative justice.
Punitive systems like policing and prisons perpetuate harm often against marginalized communities.
Alternatives to punishment include transformative and restorative justice processes driven by communities.
Mutual aid and collective organizing are essential tools in building a world without prisons or police.
Hope is a discipline that sustains abolitionist work in the face of setbacks and crises.
Incarceration and policing do not equate to safety—true safety comes from meeting people's needs and fostering community support.
Incremental reforms must not distract from the ultimate goal of dismantling oppressive systems.
notable_features: Draws on real-world organizing and lived experiences
Answers frequently asked questions about abolition with clarity and nuance
Centers voices and wisdom from activist communities
Combines theory with practical examples for building abolitionist futures
cultural_historical_context: Published amidst the resurgence of abolitionist movements, especially in the wake of the 2020 uprisings for racial justice and the growing visibility of calls to defund the police in the United States. Rooted in decades of Black feminist and abolitionist organizing.
reception_impact: Widely praised among activists, scholars, and movement organizers
Used as a teaching text in college classrooms and community workshops
Recognized for making abolitionist ideas accessible and actionable
Contributed to the mainstreaming of abolitionist discourse
Some critics argue the vision is too radical or lacks immediate policy permutations
comparable_titles: Are Prisons Obsolete? by Angela Y. Davis
Prison by Any Other Name by Maya Schenwar and Victoria Law
Abolition for the People edited by Colin Kaepernick
The End of Policing by Alex S. Vitale
